extracted.intended_audience: students learning news writing / journalism students
extracted.subtask_description: Sentence- and paragraph-level exercises from a news-writing textbook asking students to identify and correct faults (ellipsis, coherence, emphasis, phraseology, word choice, grammar) and to rewrite source material into news copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faulty ellipsis
rubrics_metrics.description: The following sentences contain errors due principally to faulty ellipsis. Point out the faults in ellipsis and correct all errors. (Mainly paragraph 166.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students are given numerous example sentences that illustrate omitted words, broken constructions, and incorrect deletion of words (anti-patterns). For each sentence identify the elliptical omission or malformed ellipsis and produce a corrected, grammatical version. Examples provided include sentences with missing verbs, dangling modifiers, and incorrect clause truncation (e.g., 'Marvin Cloudt and Ferdinand Willie attended the dance Tuesday night ... and hear they enjoyed it well and caught themselves nice sweethearts').

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconstruct sentences for clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Reconstruct the following sentences in any way that will make them clear. Point out the errors in the sentences as they now stand. (Mainly paragraphs 167-162.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate sentences for unclear reference, poor syntax, run-ons, faulty modifiers, and logical confusion; rewrite them to be clear and natural. Students may reorder clauses, supply missing information, eliminate ambiguity, and correct grammatical mistakes. Numerous example items show typical newspaper-era problems (awkward chronology, misplaced modifiers, confusing apposition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewrite to improve coherence
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewrite the following sentences in any way that will improve their coherence (mainly paragraphs 163-164).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify incoherent or disjointed phrasing and produce rewrites that improve logical flow, sentence linkage, and readability. Guidance is illustrated by long, tangled sentences that need segmentation, tightened transitions, or reordering of information to produce coherent news prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improve emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: The following sentences lack emphasis. Explain why and improve the emphasis in each. (Paragraphs 166-168.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine why a sentence fails to highlight its most important element (weak word order, buried subject, hedging, excess verbiage) and rewrite to place the key idea in a strong syntactic position (e.g., fronting, active voice, short clauses). Examples include diluted leads, passive constructions that hide actors, and sentences that bury the news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fix crude or affected phraseology (unemphatic due to phraseology)
rubrics_metrics.description: The following sentences are unemphatic because of their crude or affected phraseology. Rewrite each so that it shall be good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace clichéd, overwritten, pompous, or awkward expressions with plain, effective journalistic language. Identify affected rhetorical flourishes, mixed metaphors, overlong adjectival strings, and archaic diction and render concise, appropriate alternatives. Examples include ornate descriptive passages and inflated metaphors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish meanings of similar words
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish the meanings of the words in the following groups (e.g., Abscond, avoid, decamp, elude, escape, evade; Accident, calamity, casualty, disaster, mishap, misfortune; etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate precise word-choice ability by explaining nuanced differences among near-synonyms and selecting the most appropriate term for journalistic contexts. This trains reporters to avoid imprecise or misleading vocabulary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide equivalents (simplify phrases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Give equivalents for [a list of overlong or clichéd phrases] (e.g., 'doing as well as can be expected', 'blushing bride', 'first number on the program', 'goes without saying', etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convert wordy, conventional, or pompous expressions into concise, idiomatic alternatives suitable for news copy. The page lists many stock phrases to be replaced with clearer equivalents; use these as practice in tightening prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct sentences (usage, grammar, logic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Correct the following: [a long numbered list of faulty sentences].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and fix grammatical errors, faulty agreement, awkward constructions, incorrect idiom, logical inconsistencies, punctuation problems, and poor ordering. Examples include misplaced modifiers, incorrect pronoun references, mixed constructions, improper tense/aspect, and factual-clarity issues. Students should produce corrected versions and note the original error type for each item.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write up source material into a news story
rubrics_metrics.description: Write up the story for an Indianapolis morning paper on which you are working using provided materials (e.g., a speech by George Ade and a New York dispatch about the dinner).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice converting raw source material (speech text and dispatch) into a news article suitable for a specific paper: choose an appropriate lead, select and prioritize facts, paraphrase quotations, localize the angle for the paper's audience (George Ade's Indiana ties), and adhere to concise, objective news-writing style. This item illustrates synthesizing disparate inputs into a coherent news item.
